title: Two · why slow works
text: Part two · why slow works

title: Two · why slow works
section: The heart is already breathing with you
text:
The heart is already breathing with you

Now, in you


Your heart rate is not steady. It rises as you breathe in and falls as you breathe out, and it is doing that at this moment.


The research Lehrer & Gevirtz, 20141, and Russo and colleagues, 20172. The pattern has a name — respiratory sinus arrhythmia — and the 2014 review states it plainly: heart rate “increases during inhalation and decreases during exhalation”.
As solid as anything on these pages. It is directly observable in anyone, with any device that reads a pulse, and it needs no statistics at all.


Move through one breath. The direction is the established finding; the size of the swing drawn here is illustrative, because yours depends on your age, your fitness and how slowly you are breathing.

If you have ever put a pulse oximeter on someone and watched the number wander, this is what you were watching. It is not the device being imprecise.
Why it happens is a longer story than it looks, and the 2014 review is careful to say that parts of the account are proposed rather than settled. The short version is that the same brainstem machinery times the breath and adjusts the heart, and that the pressure sensors in the big arteries — the baroreflex — are correcting blood pressure continuously as the chest changes shape around them.
The useful part for a practitioner is simpler. The breath is not a separate system you are reaching in to influence. It is already wired to the heart, continuously, in everyone, and what a breathing instruction does is change the timing of something that is happening anyway.

For your hands This is the one claim on the page a client can check for themselves in thirty seconds with a finger on their own wrist and a long slow breath. Things people verify on their own body land differently from things they are told.

title: Two · why slow works
section: One rate rings louder than the others
text:
One rate rings louder than the others

2014


Breathe at about six a minute and the swing in your heart rate gets much bigger. Not gradually bigger as you slow down — biggest at one particular rate, and smaller again either side of it.


The research Lehrer & Gevirtz, 20141. “Maximum heart rate oscillations at respiratory frequency occurred at approximately 0.1 Hz (six breaths per minute)”, refined in the same review to about 5.5 a minute, a breath of roughly eleven seconds. Russo’s review reports the same peak2.
Where the peak sits is replicated and solid. The mechanism has a good account — and the authors of the review are explicit that parts of it are speculation, including the newer suggestion about signals travelling up the vagus nerve to the front of the brain.


Find the peak. Where it sits is the established finding; the height of the hill is drawn rather than measured, and how sharp yours is will not be quite this.

Here is the part that makes it a resonance rather than just a good rate. Your blood pressure is being corrected continuously by the baroreflex, and that correction takes a few seconds to arrive. Breathe at around six a minute and each breath’s push lands just as the correction from the last one comes through — heart rate and blood pressure end up running half a cycle apart, blood pressure falling as heart rate rises. The timing is what does it: every push adds to the swing already there instead of fighting it.
It is the same reason a child on a swing goes higher when the pushes are timed to the swing rather than delivered faster. The system has a natural period, and matching it costs nothing and does more.
What this does not establish is what people usually go on to say. A bigger swing in heart rate is a real physiological change, and it is a measurement, not an outcome. The step from this makes your heart rate variation larger to this makes you healthier is the step part three is about, and it is much less secure than this stop.

For your hands If you are going to give someone a number, six a minute is the one with the most behind it — in through the nose for about four seconds, out for about six, and no straining at either end. Longer out than in is the part most people find easiest to hold on to.

title: Two · why slow works
section: And it is not the same rate for everybody
text:
And it is not the same rate for everybody

2006


Six a minute is the average of a spread, not a setting. People have their own rate, it can be found, and it stays put.


The research Vaschillo, Vaschillo & Lehrer, 20063 — 32 adults with asthma and 24 healthy adults, each tested to find the rate at which their own heart rate swung most.
One laboratory, 56 people, and the findings are reported as directions rather than as numbers — which is why the figure shows directions and no numbers. Good enough to say the spread is real and roughly what predicts it. Not good enough to give anyone a formula.


What predicted a person’s own best rate, and what did not. No numbers on this figure, deliberately — the paper does not publish the coefficients and inventing them would be worse than leaving them out.

Taller people resonated at a slower rate, and men slower than women — which is very likely the same finding twice, since the paper relates it to blood volume rather than to sex as such. Age did not predict it. Weight did not. Having asthma did not.
And the finding that matters most for anyone teaching this: a person’s rate stayed the same across ten sessions. It is a stable property of them, like a resting heart rate, rather than something that moves with their mood or how the day has gone.
So the honest version of “breathe at six a minute” is: six is a good place to start, your own best rate is probably within a breath or two either side of it, and the way to find it is to try a few and notice which one feels like it takes the least effort to keep going.

For your hands If six feels wrong for someone — strained, or oddly effortful — that is worth taking at face value rather than as a failure to relax. Try five and try seven. Bigger people tend to sit at the slower end.

title: Breathing is not a switch
text:
A reading journey for hands-on practitioners

Breathing is not a switch

Breathing is the one part of the autonomic nervous system you can take hold of directly. That is genuinely remarkable, and it is why every tradition that works with bodies has found its way to the breath.
It has also made the breath the most oversold thing in the field. Somewhere between the real physiology and the workshop version, “slow down and breathe out for longer” turned into switching your nervous system between states, and the second one is not something anyone can currently support.



This is a reading journey through what is established, in a series of short stops and about half an hour. Every figure can be operated. Every claim names its source before you meet it, and says how much that source can carry.
The good news arrives early and it is better than the oversold version: there really is a rate at which the heart and the blood vessels and the breath fall into step, it is findable, and it is about six breaths a minute. Most of this page is that, and what it is not.


Who it is for
Massage therapists, bodyworkers, physiotherapists, nurses, yoga and movement teachers, somatic practitioners — anyone who has ever said and now just breathe to a person on a table, and wondered afterwards exactly what they were claiming.
No science background needed. Where a technical word is the right one, we introduce it and say what it means in ordinary language beside it.


What is here
One · what breathing is doing. What an ordinary rate looks like, why the lungs are not where the interesting part happens, and what goes wrong when you breathe more than the body asked for.
Two · why slow works. The heart is already following your breath. One rate makes that swing largest, for a reason that has a decent account behind it — and that rate is not the same for everybody.
Three · being honest about it. What breathwork does in randomised trials, which is real and modest, and how much weight each thing here can carry.
What we carry back. What we came away with, and every source in the order the journey met them.


Nothing here is medical advice. Anyone with a heart or lung condition, or who is pregnant, should take breathing exercises up with a clinician rather than with a web page.

Before you start If you take one thing from this: slower is the active ingredient, not deeper. A great deal of what follows is that sentence, with the evidence attached — and one stop about what deeper on its own can actually do.

title: Three · being honest about it
text: Part three · being honest about it

title: Three · being honest about it
section: What it measurably does
text:
What it measurably does

2023


Somebody gathered the randomised trials of breathwork and pooled them. The effect is real, it is small-to-medium, and the authors went out of their way to warn against the version of their own result that was about to get quoted.


The research Fincham, Strauss, Montero-Marin & Cavanagh, 20231. From 1325 initial results they took randomised controlled trials only: 12 trials and 785 adults for stress, 20 for anxiety, 18 for low mood.
The best evidence on the question, and the authors say most of the trials were at moderate risk of bias — which for a breathing intervention is close to unavoidable, since nobody can be blinded to how they are breathing. Their own closing sentence asks for better research “to avoid a miscalibration between hype and evidence.”


Only stress has a published confidence interval, so only stress gets a bar. The other two are drawn as bare points, because a made-up interval would be a worse figure than an incomplete one.

Stress came out at a standardised effect of −0.35, somewhere between −0.55 and −0.14. Anxiety came out at −0.32 and low mood at −0.40, both better than the control conditions — though the abstract publishes no interval for either, which is why the figure draws them as bare points.
In plain terms: this works, and it works about as well as a decent self-help intervention works. It is not nothing and it is not transformative. If somebody leaves your room breathing more slowly than they arrived, you have done something worth doing, and you have not rewired them.
Two limits worth carrying. Every one of these outcomes is self-reported — how people say they feel, which is the easiest thing in the field to shift and also the thing that matters most to them. And “breathwork” pools a lot of quite different practices, which is part of why the trials disagree with each other.

For your hands The evidence supports offering this warmly and describing it modestly. “This reliably helps people feel less stressed, by a useful amount” is well within what the trials show. Anything about states, systems or rewiring is not.

title: Three · being honest about it
section: How much each of these can carry
text:
How much each of these can carry

Now


Every stop on this page rests on a source, and the sources are not equally good. Flattening that would undo most of the point of writing it down.


The research All of it, weighed against each other. The placement below is our judgement, not a measurement, and the caption says so — what it is for is the ordering.
The bottom entry has no source at all, which is the honest way to record it. “Breathing technique changes long-run health” is the claim that sells the workshops, and we could not find trials that establish it. Its absence is a finding.


A judgement, not a measurement. The value is the gradient: the best-supported claims are the ones you can check on your own wrist, and the one with the most riding on it sits at the bottom with nothing under it.

Notice the shape. The top of this list is made of things that are directly observable — your heart rate follows your breath; the swing is largest around six a minute. They need no trial because you can watch them happen.
The bottom is where the money is. Breathing technique changes long-run health is the claim that fills rooms, and there is no adequate evidence for it — not evidence against it, which is a different thing, but an absence where the trials would be. That is worth saying out loud precisely because everything above it is so solid. A page that establishes four real things is not licensed to wave the fifth through.

For your hands The strongest thing you can offer is also the most checkable: a rate, a reason, and something the person can verify on their own pulse. It is a smaller claim than the one they may have heard, and it has the advantage of being true.

title: One · what pain is
text: Part one · what pain is

title: One · what pain is
section: More people than any other complaint
text:
More people than any other complaint

2023


Low back pain is the largest single cause of disability on earth. Not the most dangerous, not the most expensive to treat — the one that takes the most life away from the most people.


The research The Global Burden of Disease study, 2021 cycle, published in 20231. Population studies from 204 countries, run through a Bayesian model to fill the gaps.
Strong for the ordering and the direction, softer for any single number — the authors say plainly that country-level primary data is thin and that they need better. The uncertainty intervals in the figure are theirs, not ours.


Counts, with the range the study itself gives. Turn the uncertainty off to see how much more confident a bare headline number looks than the evidence behind it.

In 2020 about 619 million people were living with low back pain, and the study projects 843 million by 2050. Both of those come with a range, and the range is wide enough to matter: the 2020 figure could be anywhere from 554 to 694 million.
The more interesting number is the one that went the other way. Over the same thirty years the age-standardised rate — roughly, one person’s chance of having back pain — fell by about 10%. More people have it and each person is slightly less likely to. The world got bigger and older, which is a different story from an epidemic, and worth having ready when someone repeats the epidemic version.
About 39% of the disability was attributed to occupational factors, smoking and high body mass together. Which leaves most of it not attributed to any of them.

For your hands The scale is worth knowing because it reframes the room. A person with back pain is not an unusual case with something rare going on. They are the most ordinary presentation in the world, and the base rate for “nothing sinister” is very high.

title: One · what pain is
section: An experience, not a reading
text:
An experience, not a reading

2020


The field that studies pain spent two years arguing about how to define it, and the definition it landed on does not mention damage as a requirement.


The research Raja and colleagues, 20202 — the report of the International Association for the Study of Pain’s task force, fourteen people over two years, revising a definition that had stood since 1979.
Not an experiment, and it should not be quoted as one. It is the field writing down what it agrees on, which is a different kind of evidence and a useful one: it tells you what is no longer controversial.

The revised definition reads:

An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage.

Four words were added — or resembling that associated with — and they carry most of the change. Pain can occur with damage. It can occur with the threat of damage. And it can occur with neither, and still be pain, and still be exactly as unpleasant.

A diagram of that definition, not a measurement. The weights behind the switches are illustrative — no study assigns them, and the figure would be dishonest if it pretended otherwise. What is not illustrative is the shape: the signal on the left does not change.

Two words worth separating, because most confusion here is the two being used interchangeably. Nociception is the signalling — nerve endings responding to pressure, heat, or chemistry, and sending something up the cord. Pain is what a person experiences. They usually travel together. They are not the same thing, and either can happen without the other.
That is not a philosophical nicety. It is why the same injury hurts differently on a Tuesday morning and at two in the morning, why a footballer finishes the match, and why a person whose scan has not changed in three years can hurt more this month than last.

For your hands When someone asks why does it hurt so much if nothing is broken, the honest answer is that hurting a lot and being broken a lot are two different measurements, and the second one is not what the first one reports.

title: One · what pain is
section: What happens on the way in
text:
What happens on the way in

1965 · revised since


A signal from the body is not delivered intact. It arrives at a junction where other traffic is arriving too, and what continues upward depends on what else showed up.


The research Melzack & Wall, 19653 — gate control theory, one of the most influential papers in the field. And Mendell, 20144, a review by someone who worked on the original, setting out what survived of it and what did not.
Foundational, and much revised. The 1965 circuit diagram should not be presented as current detail — several of its specifics turned out to be wrong. That signals are modulated before they arrive is not in doubt at all.


Take the hand off the skin and watch the same pain signal get further. The gate is a simplification of a much-revised mechanism; the modulation it stands for is real.

Rubbing a banged shin is not a distraction technique and it is not a placebo. The large, fast fibres that carry touch reach the same junction in the spinal cord as the thin, slow fibres carrying the pain signal, and their arrival changes what is passed on. The hand goes to the shin before anyone decides to send it.
What 1965 got right was the principle: there is a control point, and the volume is set there rather than at the skin. What it got wrong was much of the wiring, and the field spent decades correcting it. Modern accounts also add something the original barely had — signals coming down from the brain that open and close the same gate, which is where expectation and attention get their hands on the dial.

For your hands A great deal of hands-on work is arriving at that junction with competing traffic. That is a real mechanism and worth saying out loud. It is also not a claim that you are releasing anything, correcting anything, or removing a cause.

title: Two · how loose the link is
text: Part two · how loose the link is
crumbs: Two · how loose the link is

title: Two · how loose the link is
section: What a back looks like when nothing hurts
text:
What a back looks like when nothing hurts

2015


Somebody gathered every study that had scanned people with no back pain at all, and counted how many of them had the findings that get blamed for back pain.


The research Brinjikji and colleagues, 20151. Thirty-three studies, 3110 people with no symptoms, thirty-two of the studies using MRI. Prevalence by decade comes from a model fitted across the studies, so these are estimates rather than counts.
Solid, and the single most useful thing on this page. Its limits are the authors’ own: many participants were volunteers rather than a random sample, agreement between radiologists reading the same scan is moderate at best, the studies span more than 25 years, and — this one matters — the findings were not sorted by severity. Pain-free people may simply have milder versions.


Drag the age. Every number is the percentage of people with no back pain who have that finding on a scan. The figure cannot tell you these never matter — only how ordinary they are in people who feel fine.

At twenty, more than a third of pain-free people already have disc degeneration. By sixty it is 88%, and by eighty, 96%. Disc bulges: 30% of pain-free twenty-year-olds, 84% of pain-free eighty-year-olds. Wear at the small joints behind the spine goes from 4% to 83% across the same span.
Put plainly: for most of these findings, having one is the normal condition of a human back of that age, and finding one on a scan of somebody in pain does not establish that it is the reason.
This is where the honest version has to hold two things at once, and it would be easy to drop one. These findings are not nothing — some of them, in some people, are genuinely part of the problem, and the authors say explicitly that imaging must be read against the patient in front of you. What the data rules out is the automatic inference: scan looks worn, therefore worn is why it hurts.

For your hands Somebody will show you a report with words like degeneration, bulge and wear on it, and they will be frightened. The figure above is a good thing to have seen, because it lets you say something true and calming at once: those words describe most backs of that age, including the ones that feel fine. It is not your place to reinterpret their imaging — but it is entirely reasonable to say that the words are more ordinary than they sound.
crumbs: Two · how loose the link is

title: Two · how loose the link is
section: The same cold, two colours
text:
The same cold, two colours

2007


A very cold rod was put on people’s hands. The rod was identical every time. The only thing that changed was a coloured light, and how much it hurt changed with it.


The research Moseley & Arntz, 20072. A rod at −20 °C on one hand for half a second, paired with either a red light, described as hot and more tissue-damaging, or a blue one, described as cold and less damaging.
A well-designed laboratory experiment with a large effect, and a laboratory stimulus — half a second of cold on a hand is not a bad back. The abstract reports the differences between conditions rather than a score for each, and it reports them as approximate. It does not report how many people took part, so we do not state a number.


Switch the light. The rod does not change. The paper reports the gap between the two conditions rather than a score for each, so the pair is drawn around the middle of the scale — the distance between them is the measured thing.

With the red light, people rated the same freezing rod as roughly five and a half points hotter on an eleven-point scale. Not more unpleasant in general — hotter. The sensation itself reported differently.
They also rated it about three and a half points more unpleasant and about three points more intense. Those three numbers are separable on purpose: the study was designed to show that context does not simply turn one dial, it moves the sensory reading and the emotional reading somewhat independently.
The stimulus was cold. Believing it was hot and dangerous made it feel hot. That is not suggestibility or poor reporting — it is what the definition in part one describes, showing up in a measurement.

For your hands Everything a person believes about what is happening to their tissue is part of what they feel. When you name a finding, describe a technique, or explain what you think is going on, you are not adding commentary to a sensation that is already fixed. You are inside the thing that determines it.

title: Four · being honest about it
text: Part four · being honest about it

title: Four · being honest about it
section: What teaching people this actually does
text:
What teaching people this actually does

2026


This whole page is an argument for explaining pain to people. So it is only fair to ask what happens when somebody does that in a trial, and the answer is: less than the field would like.


The research Khan and colleagues, 20261 — a systematic review and meta-analysis of pain neuroscience education, which is the formal name for teaching people roughly what parts one to three of this page teach. Twelve randomised trials, 1485 people.
The most honest number on this page. The effect on pain intensity is small, and its confidence interval reaches exactly zero — the trials also disagreed with each other a great deal. The sleep result is cleaner and the trials agreed on it. Read as a whole: this does something, and it is not the large effect the enthusiasm around it suggests.


The bar is where the true effect probably sits. The pain bar reaches zero, which means “no effect at all” has not been ruled out. The sleep bar does not reach it.

The pain result is a standardised effect of −0.27, with a range from −0.50 to 0.00. In plain terms: on average people hurt somewhat less, the effect is small, and the evidence is compatible with it doing nothing to pain at all. The trials also disagreed substantially among themselves, which usually means the thing being tested was not the same thing in every trial.
Total sleep time came out at +0.42, from 0.12 to 0.71, and there the trials agreed with each other completely. It is the sturdier finding, and it is not the one anybody advertises.
We could have left this stop out. The page would have read better and been worse. If the argument is check what the evidence actually says, that has to include checking it on the thing the page is itself doing.

For your hands Explaining pain well is worth doing, and it is not a treatment on its own. The trials that did best combined it with movement and with the rest of care — which is roughly what you were going to do anyway.

title: Four · being honest about it
section: How much each of these can carry
text:
How much each of these can carry

Now


Every stop on this page rests on a source, and the sources are not equally good. Flattening that would undo most of the point.


The research All of it, weighed against each other. The placement below is our judgement, not a measurement, and the caption says so — what it is for is the ordering.
The last entry deserves naming. A builder jumped onto a plank and a seven-inch nail went through his boot. He was in agony and was sedated before the boot came off, at which point the nail turned out to have passed cleanly between his toes without touching him2. It is a wonderful story, and it is one paragraph in a magazine column — no method, no follow-up, no imaging — retold in more lectures than most randomised trials.


A judgement, not a measurement. The value is the gradient: the best-supported things are the least dramatic, and the most repeated story on the page sits at the bottom.

Notice the shape of it. The claims near the top are boring — findings that look like damage are common in people with no pain, signals are turned up and down on the way in. The claims near the bottom are the ones that make a good lecture. That is not a coincidence and it is not unique to this field, but it is worth being able to see.
The nail story is a good test of your own habits. It probably persuaded you when you first heard it, and it should not have — not because it is false, but because a paragraph cannot carry the weight of a general claim about how pain works. The scans in part two carry that weight. The nail carries almost none of it, and gets repeated ten times as often.

For your hands When you find yourself reaching for the most memorable example, check what it is made of. The strongest thing you can say to a frightened client is not the dramatic anecdote — it is the boring, replicated one about what ordinary backs look like.

title: One · the territory
text: Part one · the territory

title: One · the territory
section: There are two ways of being touched
text:
There are two ways of being touched

The idea


Everything else here follows from one thing: touch is not a single sense. Two separate kinds of nerve fibre leave the skin at the same instant, travelling at very different speeds, and they are not carrying the same message.


The research This first stop is the shared framework rather than a single study — it is drawn from the review by McGlone, Wessberg & Olausson (2014)1, which is also the best single thing to read after this page.


The animation runs in real time. A fast signal crosses in a few hundredths of a second; the slow one takes about a second. That gap is the finding itself, not an effect added to illustrate it.

The fast road is the one most people mean by touch. Thick fibres wrapped in myelin, an insulating sheath that lets a signal race along at tens of metres per second. They are superb at what and where — the exact spot, the texture, the pressure, the edge of the object in your hand. This is the system that lets you find a coin in your pocket without looking.
The slow road is the surprise. Thin fibres with no insulation, a signal ambling along at about one metre per second — so slow that when someone strokes your forearm, that part of the message arrives something like a second behind the rest. They are poor at what and where. What they seem to carry, instead, is how it feels.
Those two colours — blue for the fast road, clay for the slow one — mean the same thing in every figure from here on. Nothing below assumes you have met any of this before.

For your hands If you have ever wondered why a client goes quiet a beat after your hands land rather than as they land, there is a real signal running about a second behind the obvious one.

title: One · the territory
section: You are working on a sense organ, not a covering
text:
You are working on a sense organ, not a covering

Where it happens


Skin is usually described as a barrier. It is also the largest sensory surface you have, and the fast road alone arrives on four different kinds of receptor, each answering to something different.


The research Standard anatomy rather than a finding2 — the classification of mechanoreceptors below is textbook material, and each type links to its Wikipedia entry if you want the detail.


Depths and shapes are schematic. Tap a receptor to read what it does.

Tap any receptor in the diagram. Two live near the surface and handle fine, quick things: Merkel cells for edges and texture, and Meissner corpuscles for slip — the receptor that tells you a glass is sliding out of your grip before you consciously notice.
Two sit deeper and handle slower, coarser things. Ruffini endings register stretch across the skin, part of how you know where your hand is without looking. Pacinian corpuscles register fast vibration, which is how you feel the texture of a surface through the end of a tool rather than through your fingertips.
And then the fifth kind: bare nerve endings with no capsule at all, wandering in the hairy skin. Those are the slow road, and the next four stops are about them.

For your hands When you change from a fingertip to a flat palm, from gliding to holding, from still to vibrating, you are not adjusting an intensity. You are moving between different receptors with different jobs.

title: One · the territory
section: Your fingertips are fifteen times sharper than your back
text:
Your fingertips are fifteen times sharper than your back

How fine


How close together can two points be before skin stops feeling them as two? The answer varies across the body by more than fifteen-fold — and the conclusion people usually draw from that is wider than the measurement allows.


The research The numbers everyone quotes come from Weinstein’s 1968 survey3. The test itself has been questioned for years as a measure of how finely you can feel4 — the ranking across the body is solid, the exact millimetres softer than they look.


Drawn larger than life so the smallest gaps stay visible; the proportions between body parts are the real ones. Values are the classic Weinstein figures, widely reproduced — the ranking is solid, the exact millimetres less so.

Pick a body part and look at the gap drawn to scale. On a fingertip the two dots have to come within two or three millimetres before they merge into one. On the back they can be nearly four centimetres apart and still feel like a single touch. This is two-point discrimination, and it tracks how densely the fast receptors are packed.
It is tempting to conclude from this that precision on a back is pointless. That would be over-reading a very narrow measurement, in at least three ways. Locating a single contact is generally more accurate than telling two apart, so a person can often say roughly where your hand is even where they could not resolve two touches. Pressure reaches past the skin — muscle, fascia and joints have their own sensory supply, and where you press changes what you are pressing on whatever the skin can resolve. And the precision may matter most to you: feeling your way is information travelling to you, the practitioner, and your fingertips resolve at two or three millimetres.
What the number does tell you is narrower and still worth having: do not expect fine surface detail on a back to be perceived as detail by the person receiving it. And treat the exact figures gently — people can sometimes report “two” when both points are in the same place, which suggests the task picks up cues besides spacing.

For your hands Try it on yourself with two pencil tips or a bent paperclip. Fingertip, forearm, back. Then have someone touch one spot on your back and point to where you think it was — you will usually be closer than the two-point figure would suggest.

title: Touch is not one sense
text:
A reading journey for hands-on practitioners

Touch is not one sense

Skin carries at least two separate systems, and they are not sending the same message. One tells you what you are touching. The other answers mainly to being touched affectionately. It was found by accident, confirmed by a man who had lost the ordinary sense of touch, and it fires hardest at one particular speed.



This is a reading journey through the research on touch — the sense, not the technique — in a series of short stops and about half an hour. Every figure can be operated. Every claim names its source before you meet it, and says how much that source can carry.
What follows is what we found reading our way through it: what each system responds to, what touch does to pain and to relationships, and which of the popular claims we could not get to stand up.


Who it is for
Anyone whose work involves putting hands on other people: massage therapists, bodyworkers, physiotherapists, osteopaths, nurses, midwives, somatic and trauma practitioners. No science background is assumed — we did not begin with much of one either.
Every claim points to a named paper, cited at the top of its section and listed at the foot of the page it appears on, so you can go and check where we have read it wrong. And where researchers disagree, which here they do a good deal, we have tried to say so rather than pick a side.


What is here
One · the territory. Two roads, the receptors they arrive on, and how finely skin can actually resolve what it feels.
Two · the second system. How the slow road was found, the patient who proved it carries an experience, and the two things it is tuned to.
Three · what touch does. Pain, the map of who may touch you where, and an honest sorting of how sure anyone can be about any of it.
Four · being honest about it. Four things the field has had to take back, and why the fibre is not the feeling.
What we carry back into the room. What we came away with, where to go next, and every source in the order the journey met them.


Nothing here is medical advice, and nothing here is a technique manual. It is a record of what two readers found in the literature, assembled in 2026 from the literature as it stood — and it cannot tell you what the person in front of you wants.

Before you start If you take one thing from this: the same touch is not the same experience. Most of what follows is the two systems and what each of them answers to — slow, warm, moving contact on hairy skin. Part four is about why that turns out to be the smaller half.

title: Four · being honest about it
text: Part four · being honest about it

title: Four · being honest about it
section: Four things this field has had to take back
text:
Four things this field has had to take back

2021–2023


Everything in part two is a decade old or more, and parts of it have been revised. A practitioner quoting the 2014 version is now quoting something the researchers have moved on from.


The research Six papers between 2021 and 2023, named on the cards: Watkins1, Case2, Ali3, Bendas4, Crucianelli5 and — the largest — Schirmer, Croy & Ackerley6, a review by researchers inside the field checking their own published work.


Four corrections from the last decade. Tap each card to turn it over.

None of these demolish the story. They complicate it in ways that mostly make it more useful, and they are worth knowing so that you are not the last person in the room still saying the old version.
The fourth is the largest and the least comfortable. Going through the literature, the authors found that of the papers using the phrase “affective touch”, only 34% even mention these fibres. A nerve fibre and a human experience had quietly become the same word, and they are not the same thing.

For your hands When you explain your work, describe the touch — slow, light, warm, moving, on a forearm — rather than claiming to activate a named nerve fibre. The first is accurate and checkable; the second goes further than anyone can currently support.

title: Four · being honest about it
section: The fibre is not the feeling
text:
The fibre is not the feeling

Now


The most useful correction of all, and it comes from within the research rather than from its critics.


The research Sailer & Leknes (2022)7 and Schirmer, Croy & Schweinberger (2022)8. Position pieces rather than experiments — arguments about how to read the evidence, from people who generated much of it. Under them sit two studies that held the touch still and changed only what the person believed: Gazzola (2012)9 and Ellingsen (2013)10.
Both are small and both are awkward, and they are worth having anyway. Gazzola ran eighteen heterosexual men, and the man in the video behaved distantly where the woman behaved warmly — so belief about sex, about attractiveness and about manner all arrive together and cannot be pulled apart. Ellingsen’s effects on pleasantness are a fifth of a point, and its comparison session involved no spray at all, so nobody was in the dark about which session they were in. What survives in both is the thing we came for: the contact at the skin never changed, and what people felt did.


Two halves, and they are not the same kind of thing. Above the line it is illustrative — no study assigns those verdict words, and they are there because the point is hard to feel from a sentence and easy to feel from a switch. Below the line it is measured.

The same stroke, at the same speed and the same temperature, is not the same experience depending on who is doing it, whether you consented, what happened last time, and what you believe it is for. One paper’s title puts it plainly: meaning makes touch affective. The other argues that social touch is better understood as a tool people use to do something to each other than as a signal being transmitted.
This is more than an argument. In one study, eighteen men were stroked on the forearm by the same woman every time — she could not see which video was playing — while they were shown who was supposedly touching them. Believing it was a man, they rated it −2.53. Believing it was a woman, +3.05, on a scale running from −5 to +5. And the primary somatosensory cortex — the usual place, where the fast road arrives and the map of the skin is laid out — responded more strongly as well. Belief was not sitting on top of the sensation, interpreting it after the fact. It reached the place the signal arrives first.
The second study is quieter. People watched a short film about oxytocin, then sprayed salt water up their own noses believing it might be the hormone. Pleasant touch was rated a little better, painful heat a little less bad — and in the brain the two moved in opposite directions, sensory activity rising for the pleasure and falling for the pain. Whatever expectation is doing, it is not turning one volume knob down.
None of this is a demotion of the nerve fibres. It is a description of where they sit. They look like a doorway — a channel well suited to carrying this kind of contact. What comes through the doorway is decided by everything else.
Which is, if you think about it, what a good practitioner already knows. The biology has caught up with the room.

For your hands Speed and warmth are worth getting right, and they are the smaller half. Consent, predictability, and whether the person wanted to be touched by you are doing more work than any number on this page.

title: What we carry back into the room
text: Closing

title: What we carry back into the room
section: What we would carry back into the room
text:
What we would carry back into the room

The end of it


What we came away with, loosely ordered by how much weight we would put on each. Not instructions — a record of what the reading suggested.


The research Everything cited on the previous pages, weighed as part three weighs it. Nothing new is introduced here.


The figure from part four, repeated because it is the thing to leave with. Everything physical about the touch stays where it is; only what it is taken to mean changes.



Slower than feels natural — about a hand’s width a second.
One to ten centimetres a second is where the research clusters, and it is slower than most of us work by default.
Warmth seems to matter about as much as speed.
Around skin temperature — hands, oil, room. Cold shifted every speed toward less pleasant, and technique did not appear to make up for it.
Hairy skin looks like the home ground, though not the only ground.
Forearm, back, shoulders. The palm has some of these fibres after all — just fewer.
Still contact seems to count.
Resting a hand is not a lesser version of stroking. It may be preferred to stroking done wrong.
What you are trying to do decides which system you are working with.
Fine detail comes through a fingertip on hairless skin. Contact and comfort come through a broad, slow, warm hand on hairy skin.
Averages describe populations, not the person on the table.
The curve is an average across a lot of people. We would ask, watch and adjust rather than put a number on someone.
Saying what you are about to do matters more than we expected.
You have access the social map normally saves for the people we are closest to. Saying it out loud seems to be how that stays safe rather than just allowed.
Describing the touch travels further than describing the mechanism.
“Slow, warm, light, moving” is honest and checkable. “Activating your C-tactile fibres” goes beyond the evidence.
The hormone claims are the ones we would hold most loosely.
That evidence is the thinnest thing here. The pain and comfort findings are steadier and need no help from it.
Most of the work is probably not being done by the fibres.
Safety, consent, predictability and relationship. The fibres are the doorway, not the visit.



For your hands If someone leaves your room with one thing, we would want it to be the touch rather than the mechanism: slow, warm, unhurried, and from someone they agreed to be touched by. That is the part with the most behind it, and it is the part they will remember.

title: What we carry back into the room
section: Every source, in the order the journey met them
text:
Every source, in the order the journey met them

The whole list


Every source the journey cites, and where we would send someone who wants to go further. Where a paper can be read without paying for it, the link goes to the free version.


The research Everything cited above, and two entries that are not cited anywhere: Morrison (2010) and Suvilehto (2023) are in the list because they are worth reading, not because a claim on these pages rests on them.


Four corrections the field has made to its own published work, kept in view on the way out. A literature that revises itself in the open is the reason the rest of this list is worth anything.

Where to go next, in the order we would send someone.

McGlone et al. (2014) — The standard overview, free to read, and the source most people are quoting second-hand. Long, but the first half is very approachable.
Morrison et al. (2010) — The friendliest conceptual framing of why any of this might matter.
Kidd et al. (2023) — The bridge from nerve fibres to stress physiology, and the closest thing to a review written for people who do this for a living.
Suvilehto et al. (2023) — The widest recent view — who touches whom, where, and what for.


Assembled in 2026 from the literature as it stood. A reading of published research, written for people who work with touch. It is not medical advice, it does not describe a technique, and it cannot tell you what the person in front of you wants. Where researchers disagree we have tried to say so rather than tidy it away — that is not hedging, it is the current state of a young field still arguing productively with itself.


The list below is numbered in the order the journey met each source, so it reads as a record of the route rather than an alphabetical index. Each page also carries its own references at the foot, numbered for that page.

title: Two · the second system
text: Part two · the second system

title: Two · the second system
section: Someone put a needle in a nerve and listened
text:
Someone put a needle in a nerve and listened

1999


The second road was found by a group in Gothenburg who were not looking for it. The technique is microneurography, and it is exactly as unlikely as it sounds: a very fine electrode placed into a nerve in a fully awake person, listening to single fibres while their skin is touched.


The research Vallbo, Olausson & Wessberg (1999)1. Not disputed — this is the discovery, and it has held for twenty-five years.


The spike patterns are drawn to show the idea, not measured. The contrast is the real one: these fibres were told apart from pain fibres precisely by answering a gentle stimulus and not a sharp one.

Recording from forearm skin, they kept finding fibres that made no sense. They were unmyelinated — the thin, slow kind everyone associated with pain and temperature — but they responded happily to a soft brush, and hardly at all to anything sharp.
Of 38 units they picked for answering to gentle pressure on the skin, 27 were this low-threshold kind. That ratio is not a count of how common they are — the units were chosen for responding to light touch in the first place. What tells you these fibres are not rare is a separate observation: the team reported running into them about as often as the classic fast ones.
The title of the paper is the whole finding: unmyelinated fibres make up a second system for coding touch in human hairy skin. What it was doing there was completely open.

For your hands These fibres are called CT afferents. C is the slow kind with no insulating sheath, and T is for touch. That is the term you will meet everywhere else, and this is where it comes from.

title: Two · the second system
section: The man who could not feel touch, and felt it anyway
text:
The man who could not feel touch, and felt it anyway

2002


A second system is a nice idea, but how would you ever separate it from the first? The answer arrived in the form of a patient who had lost the fast road entirely.


The research Olausson and colleagues (2002)2. Strong evidence, and a single case — you cannot arrange for a second patient.




A rare nerve disease had destroyed his large, insulated fibres. On any standard test he had no sense of touch on his body: he could not feel a poke, could not say where he had been touched, could not feel vibration. The fast road was gone.
Then they stroked his forearm softly with a brush. He felt something — faint, hard to locate, and pleasant. And when they scanned his brain, the signal was not arriving at the usual place. It was lighting up the insula, a region that deals with how the body feels from the inside: hunger, warmth, breath, discomfort.
This is the study that turned an anatomical curiosity into a claim about experience. The slow road does not just exist. It goes somewhere different, and somewhere with more in common with emotion than with the map of your skin.

For your hands Affectionate touch is not a gentler version of informative touch. On this evidence it takes a different road and arrives somewhere else in the brain.

title: Two · the second system
section: And it has a favourite speed
text:
And it has a favourite speed

2009


If these fibres were built for being stroked, you would expect them to care about how fast. They do — and it is not the fastest, and it is not the slowest.


The research Löken and colleagues (2009)3. Widely replicated as a group average; individuals vary more than the tidy curve suggests, which part four returns to.


Curve shapes follow the published figure; the firing values are rough rather than exact. The dot moves at the real speed.

They brushed people’s forearms at five speeds while listening to single fibres, then asked how pleasant each stroke felt. The fast fibres did the sensible thing: the quicker the brush, the harder they fired. Speed in, speed out.
The slow fibres did something more interesting. They fired hardest at middling speeds, around one to ten centimetres a second, and less at both extremes. Drag the dial and watch the shape. It is a hill, not a ramp.
And how pleasant people rated it made the same hill. The speeds that lit up these fibres were the speeds people liked, and this range is often described as the speed of a caress. Worth a caveat that is easy to lose: when spontaneous stroking has actually been measured, it tends to run somewhat faster than the tuning peak, even though people stroke more slowly the closer they feel to the person. The hill is real. “This is exactly how humans naturally caress” is a tidier story than the measurements support.

For your hands The dot moves at the real speed. Watch it rather than the curve, then try matching it with your own hand on your forearm. That is what the research is describing.

title: Two · the second system
section: It also wants you to be warm
text:
It also wants you to be warm

2014


A second tuning, and the one most likely to change what you actually do. These fibres are fussy about temperature, and the temperature they want is skin.


The research Ackerley and colleagues (2014)4. Well supported, and a small study — as all microneurography is.


A simplified picture of two findings held together. The sweet spot is drawn as a region because that is how it behaves, not as a measured contour.

They repeated the stroking experiment at different temperatures. The fibres responded best to a brush at about 32 degrees — neutral skin temperature. Not warm. Not cool. The temperature of another person.
And the ratings followed. People found every speed more pleasant at skin temperature than at 18 degrees or at 42 degrees. Get the warmth wrong and the speed cannot rescue it.
Try the two together in the panel. The sweet spot is a small region, not a line, and both dimensions have to be right to land in it.

For your hands Cold hands are not merely unpleasant, they are the wrong stimulus. So is oil straight from a cool bottle, and so is a treatment room a couple of degrees under. This is the cheapest change on this page.

title: Three · what touch does
text: Part three · what touch does

title: Three · what touch does
section: Touch turns pain down, and company turns it down further
text:
Touch turns pain down, and company turns it down further

1965 onward


The oldest practical claim about touch, and one of the better supported. Rubbing a banged elbow is not superstition; there is a mechanism, and it was proposed sixty years ago.


The research Melzack & Wall’s gate control theory (1965)1, then Coan, Schaefer & Davidson (2006)2 and Goldstein and colleagues (2018)3. The framework is one of the field’s starting points, and much revised since; the handholding studies are small and replicated in direction.


The original 1965 drawing, much simplified. Sixty years of revision have complicated the mechanism without overturning the central claim.

The idea was that pain signals have to pass through a gate in the spinal cord on their way up, and that fast touch fibres arriving from the same patch of skin can partly close it. Signals coming down from the brain — attention, expectation, mood — can open or close it too.
The details have been revised many times in sixty years. The central claim has held: touch and pain are not independent channels, and one turns the other up or down before either reaches awareness.
Then there is who is doing the touching. When women anticipating an electric shock held someone’s hand, the threat response in the brain was reduced — less by a stranger’s hand than by their husband’s, and the better they rated the marriage, the larger the effect. Later work found that handholding during pain came with increased coupling between the two people’s brain activity, and that the more empathic the partner, the more the pain went down.

For your hands Contact can genuinely reduce pain, and it is not only about the contact — the same hand does more when it belongs to someone the person trusts. That is an argument for the relationship being part of the treatment rather than around it.

title: Three · what touch does
section: Everyone carries a map of who may touch them where
text:
Everyone carries a map of who may touch them where

2015


Not a metaphor either. Ask people to shade in which parts of their body a given person is allowed to touch, and something very orderly comes out.


The research Suvilehto and colleagues (2015)4. Large and cross-cultural, and entirely self-report — maps of what people say they would allow, which is not the same as what happens.


The zones are a simplification of the published maps; the area-against-bond relationship on the right is the paper’s actual finding.

1,368 people across five countries did exactly that, for everyone from a partner to a stranger. The maps were remarkably consistent, and the headline finding is almost embarrassingly simple: the total area a person is allowed to touch tracks the strength of the emotional bond. Cultural differences were minor.
Hands are permitted to nearly everyone. The area expands outward from there as the relationship closes, and for a stranger most of the body is off limits. The regions people guard most closely are also the regions they rate as most pleasurable to be touched on.
You occupy an unusual position on that map. As a practitioner you are given access it reserves for the people we are closest to — by agreement, in a role, for a purpose. That is a real thing to hold carefully, and it is why consent in this work is not a formality.

For your hands Your hands are on territory that, for this person, is normally reserved. Saying what you are about to do before you do it is not politeness. It is how the map gets redrawn safely.

title: Three · what touch does
section: How sure can we be about any of this?
text:
How sure can we be about any of this?

The evidence


Touch research makes a lot of claims and they are not equally supported. Here they are sorted honestly, because the strong ones get less airtime than the shaky ones.


The research This one figure is a judgement rather than any single paper’s result — a reading of the literature cited throughout, leaning on Kidd, Devine & Walker’s review5 for the stress claims and Moyer and colleagues’ meta-analysis6 for the cortisol one.


Positions are a judgement about how much weight to give each claim, not measured effect sizes. Arranged so the shape of the field is visible.

Notice the shape of it. The best-supported claims are the simplest and most physical: contact reduces pain, skin-to-skin contact steadies newborns. The weakest are the ones about hormones — the oxytocin and cortisol stories that circulate most confidently in training rooms are the ones the evidence supports least well.
That is not an accident. Subjective outcomes are easy to measure and to move; blood hormones are hard to measure, vary enormously between people and across a day, and rarely shift as neatly as the story requires. When you hear a claim about touch and a named hormone, treat it as the least secure thing in the sentence.

For your hands You do not need the hormone claims. The evidence you actually have — pain, comfort, distress, sleep in newborns — is stronger, more directly about what people come to you for, and much harder to argue with.

title: What we carry back
text: Closing

title: What we carry back
section: What we would carry back into the room
text:
What we would carry back into the room

The end of it


What we came away with. Not instructions — a record of what the reading suggested, in the order the page found them.


The research Everything cited on the previous pages, weighed as part four weighs it. Nothing new is introduced here.


The same judgement as the previous page, repeated because it is the thing to leave with.



Hurt and harm are different quantities. The amount something hurts is not a reading of how damaged it is, and the two can move independently in both directions.
A worn-looking scan is what most backs of that age look like. At sixty, 88% of people with no pain at all have disc degeneration. That does not make a finding meaningless; it makes it uninformative on its own.
What a sensation is believed to mean is part of what is felt. A −20 °C rod under a red light was rated five and a half points hotter than the same rod under a blue one.
Signals are turned up and down before they arrive. That is what a hand on a banged shin is doing, and it is a real mechanism rather than a distraction.
Long-standing pain can be a settings change rather than more damage. The gain goes up. It is also not something anyone can diagnose from a treatment room.
The words are part of the treatment. Your pelvis is out is an input, not a description. So is being unhurried, and so is being believed.
Explaining pain does something, and it is not large. Twelve trials, and the effect on pain intensity is small enough that no effect is still on the table.
The most repeated story is usually the weakest evidence. The nail through the boot is one paragraph in a magazine column and it travels further than any of the trials.
Almost nobody in front of you has something rare. Back pain is the most ordinary presentation on earth, and the base rate for nothing sinister is very high.



For your hands If a client leaves with one sentence, we would want it to be that their back is more ordinary than the report makes it sound, and that hurting is not the same as being damaged. Both of those are true, and both are the kind of true you can say without promising anything.

The whole list


Every source the journey cites. Where a paper can be read without paying for it, the link goes to the free version.


The research Everything cited above, plus nothing that was not. If a claim on this page has no number beside it, that is because we could not find a source we were willing to stand behind, and the text says so where it happens.


The most honest figure on the page, kept in view on the way out.

The reference list below is numbered in the order the journey met each source, so it reads as a record of the route rather than an alphabetical index.

title: Pain is not a damage report
text:
A reading journey for hands-on practitioners

Pain is not a damage report

Almost everyone who comes to you is in pain, and almost everyone arrives with the same model of it: something in there is broken, the amount it hurts tells you how broken, and the job is to find the break and fix it.
That model is wrong in a specific and useful way. Not wrong as in the pain is imaginary — it is as real as anything gets. Wrong as in the dial is not connected to the thing you think it is connected to.



This is a reading journey through what is established about that, in a series of short stops and about half an hour. Every figure can be operated. Every claim names its source before you meet it, and says how much that source can carry.
We wrote it for people who work with bodies and hands — massage therapists, bodyworkers, physiotherapists, nurses, movement and somatic practitioners — and for one situation in particular: the client who has been told their scan looks terrible, and believes it.


Who it is for
You do not need a science background. Where a technical word is genuinely the right one we introduce it, link it, and say what it means in ordinary language beside it.
You are also likely to have been taught some of this already, possibly in paid training, possibly with great confidence, and possibly in a version the research has since moved on from. We have tried to be careful about that. Where something is well established we say so plainly; where it is thin we say that too, and there is a whole part at the end about the claims on this page that cannot carry the weight people put on them.


What is here
One · what pain is. How much of it there is, why an experience is not a reading, and what happens to a signal on its way in.
Two · how loose the link is. What a scan of a pain-free back actually looks like, and what a coloured light does to a fixed physical stimulus.
Three · when pain stays. How a nervous system turns its own gain up, and how much of a treatment is the room rather than the technique.
Four · being honest about it. What teaching people about pain measurably does, which is less than the field would like, and how much weight each thing on this page can bear.
What we carry back. What we came away with, and every source in the order the journey met them.


Nothing here is medical advice, and nothing here is a protocol. It is a record of what two readers found in the literature, written down in the order it made sense.

Before you start If you take one thing from this, we would rather it were this: hurt and harm are different quantities. A great deal of what follows is that sentence, with the evidence attached.

title: Three · when pain stays
text: Part three · when pain stays

title: Three · when pain stays
section: The system turns its own gain up
text:
The system turns its own gain up

2011


Pain that goes on for months is often not a longer version of pain that lasts a week. The equipment doing the measuring has changed its settings.


The research Woolf, 20111 — a review by the person who named the phenomenon, in a supplement issue of Pain devoted to it.
Well established as something that happens: it can be produced deliberately in volunteers, and it shows up in brain recordings as well as in what people report. Much less settled is how much of any one person’s ongoing pain it accounts for — that step is inference, and it is argued over. Treat “central sensitisation” as a described phenomenon, not as a diagnosis you can make with your hands.


A schematic, not a measured curve from anybody. Drag the slider and watch a firm press cross into pain without the press changing. The dashed line is the same nervous system before.

The technical name is central sensitisation, and the plain version is that a nervous system carrying pain signals for long enough can become better at carrying them. The junction from part one gets more excitable. Less input is needed to produce a signal, and the same input produces more.
Two consequences a practitioner meets constantly. Things that should not hurt begin to — clothing, a light hand, a breeze. And things that should hurt a little hurt a lot. Neither is exaggeration, and neither is a sign that the tissue got worse. The curve moved.
This is genuinely good news badly delivered. A system that has turned its gain up is describing a settings change rather than more damage, and settings can change back. But notice how carefully that has to be said: the phenomenon is well described, and reading it off any individual is not. There is no test you can do in a treatment room that establishes it, and a confident diagnosis of it from a practitioner is going beyond what anyone can currently support.

For your hands If pressure that never used to hurt now does, the useful first thought is the system is reading loudly, not I found the damaged bit. It changes how hard you work, and it changes what you say about what you found.

title: Three · when pain stays
section: How much of it is the room
text:
How much of it is the room

2018


Everything that arrives with a treatment — the words, the confidence, the setting, the expectation — travels with it into the result, and some of it is doing more work than the technique.


The research Rossettini, Carlino & Testa, 20182, written for musculoskeletal practitioners and about their working conditions specifically.
A narrative review and a framework — not data, and never to be cited as an effect size. Its value is in naming the things, not in measuring them. The measured demonstration that context changes pain is the previous stop; this is the vocabulary for where it enters a treatment room.


The review’s four categories, in plain words. Nothing here carries a number, because the source does not have one — it is a map of what is in the room, not a measurement of what each part does.

The uncomfortable half of this is the nocebo side: the same channel runs in both directions. A phrase like your pelvis is out, this is the worst back I have seen today, or you should be careful with that forever is not a neutral description. It is an input to the system in the previous stop.
The comfortable half is that a practitioner has more legitimate influence here than the sceptical version of this story allows. Being unhurried, being believed, being touched by someone who seems to know what they are doing — these are not the parts of the treatment to apologise for. They are part of the treatment.
What would be dishonest is to run this the other way and conclude that technique does not matter, or that it is all in the telling. Nothing here shows that. It shows that the telling is not free.

For your hands The sentence a client repeats to their family that evening is part of what you did. Worth choosing it as deliberately as you choose where to put your hands.

title: What we carry back
text: Closing

title: What we carry back
section: What we would carry back into the room
text:
What we would carry back into the room

The end of it


What we came away with. Not instructions — a record of what the reading suggested, in the order the page found them.


The research Everything cited on the previous pages, weighed as part three weighs it. Nothing new is introduced here.


The same judgement as the previous page, repeated because it is the thing to leave with.



Slower is the active ingredient, not deeper. Almost everything established on this page follows from rate. Very little of it follows from size of breath.
Six a minute is the rate with the most behind it. A ten-second breath. Heart rate variation is largest there, and the reason it is largest there is understood.
The best rate is a property of the person. Taller people sit slower, it does not move with mood, and it stayed the same across ten sessions. Six is a starting point, not a setting.
The blood is already nearly full of oxygen. Breathing harder cannot load much more on. What your breathing changes is how readily oxygen comes off again at the far end.
Carbon dioxide is not just waste. It is part of how oxygen gets handed over. Blow off too much and the blood holds on tighter and delivers less.
Light-headed and tingling means slow the rate. It is a normal response to over-breathing, not a sign that something is wrong with the person — and they need to be told that, or they will assume it is.
Breathwork reliably reduces self-reported stress, by a useful and modest amount. Twelve randomised trials. Not nothing, not transformative.
The claim with the most riding on it has the least under it. That breathing technique changes long-run health is what fills the rooms, and the trials for it are not there.



For your hands If a client leaves with one thing, we would want it to be a number and a reason: about ten seconds a breath, because that is where the heart and the blood vessels fall into step. It is smaller than what they may have been promised elsewhere, and they can check it on their own wrist.

Every source the journey cites. Where a paper can be read without paying for it, the link goes to the free version — and for this story most of them can be.


The research Everything cited above, plus nothing that was not. Where a claim on this page has no source beside it, the text says so — the last line of the weights figure is the clearest case.

title: One · what breathing is doing
text: Part one · what breathing is doing

title: One · what breathing is doing
section: What an ordinary rate looks like
text:
What an ordinary rate looks like

2017


“Slow breathing” sounds like it must begin somewhere unusual. It begins one breath below where most people already are.


The research Russo, Santarelli & O’Rourke, 20171 — a review of the physiology of slow breathing in healthy people, written for a respiratory audience and free to read.
A review rather than an experiment, and the best single overview of this material. Its authors end by saying there is “a dire need for further research into the area”, which is worth carrying through everything below.


Drag the rate. The same number is shown as a breath length underneath, because seconds per breath is what anyone actually counts.

The review puts an ordinary resting rate at 10 to 20 breaths a minute, and defines slow breathing as 4 to 10. The two meet exactly at ten, which is the useful thing to notice: there is no gap between normal and slow, and nothing exotic is being asked for.
At six breaths a minute — the rate the rest of this page is about — a breath takes ten seconds. That is long enough to feel deliberate and short enough that most people can hold it without strain. Below about four a minute the research thins out, which is why the figure stops naming the bands there.

For your hands “Breathe slowly” is not a useful instruction, because it has no number in it. “About ten seconds a breath” is one, and someone can check themselves against it.

title: One · what breathing is doing
section: The lungs are not where the interesting part is
text:
The lungs are not where the interesting part is

Standard physiology


Breathing harder cannot load much more oxygen onto the blood, because the blood is very nearly full already. What changes with your breathing is how readily the oxygen comes off again at the far end.


The research The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve2 — textbook respiratory physiology, with no single modern source to point at, so the reference is a pointer to a standard description rather than to a study. Nothing here is contested.
The figure draws the curve from the standard equation. It is a shape, not measured data, and it is a good shape: it has been the accepted description for over a century.


Move the carbon dioxide. Watch the gap between the two dots — that gap is what actually gets handed over to the tissue, and the low end of the curve is the end that moves.

Two things are worth separating here, and almost every workshop account runs them together.
Loading. Blood leaving healthy lungs is already carrying oxygen at something like 97 or 98% of what it can hold. The top of that curve is nearly flat, so breathing harder pushes you along the flat part. There is very little headroom, which is why getting more oxygen in is not the mechanism for anything you are about to feel.
Unloading. The bottom of the curve is steep, and that is the end that responds to carbon dioxide. More carbon dioxide, and a slightly more acid blood, makes haemoglobin loosen its grip and hand oxygen over more readily. This is the Bohr effect, and it points the opposite way to most people’s intuition: carbon dioxide is not simply waste to be got rid of. It is part of how the delivery works.
So blowing off a lot of carbon dioxide shifts the whole curve leftward, and the blood holds on tighter. Oxygen-rich blood arrives at the tissue and hands over less of its load. More breathing, less delivered.
There is a real benefit at the other end of this, and the review reports it: breathing slowly at around six a minute produced a small rise in blood oxygen saturation, by using the lungs more efficiently rather than by moving more air. Slow and efficient, not fast and hard.

For your hands If someone on your table starts breathing big and fast because they were told deep breathing is good, that is not a mild version of the right thing. Slower is the ingredient. Bigger, on its own, is the next stop.

title: One · what breathing is doing
section: When more breathing is less
text:
When more breathing is less

2005


The light-headed, tingling, faintly unreal feeling that comes with over-breathing is not anxiety about the exercise. It is a measurable drop in blood flow to the brain.


The research Stocchetti and colleagues, 20053, a review of deliberately induced hyperventilation in head injury.
An odd-looking source for a page like this, and the honest one. In intensive care, hyperventilation is used on purpose to narrow blood vessels in the brain and lower the pressure inside the skull — and its known danger is cutting blood flow too far. That establishes the direction, and that the lever is large. It says nothing about the dose anyone gets on a mat, and the figure carries no dose for that reason.


Directions only, no numbers. The chain is well established; how far along it any particular person travels is not something anyone can currently put a figure on.

The chain runs: breathe more than the body is asking for → carbon dioxide in the blood falls → blood vessels in the brain narrow → less blood reaches the brain → light-headed, tingling hands and lips, a sense of unreality. Add the Bohr effect from the last stop and the blood that does arrive gives up less of its oxygen.
None of that is dangerous in a healthy person doing it briefly, and it stops when the breathing stops. It is worth knowing anyway, for two reasons. It explains a thing you will see. And it is the clearest case on this page where more of the good thing is simply a different thing.
Note what the honest version cannot say. It cannot tell you how fast is too fast, because the evidence comes from a setting where the amount is controlled by machine and measured directly. Anyone offering a threshold is going past their evidence.

For your hands Tingling hands and light-headedness in a breathing exercise are a signal to slow the rate, not to push through. The nearest thing to an antidote is an unhurried, ordinary breath — and the person needs to be told it is a normal response to over-breathing, or they will read it as something being wrong with them.
